data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time urban heat island is primarily caused by the delayed release of daytime heat stored in high thermal-mass impervious surfaces, and the cross-city magnitude of the gap scales with sky-view factor: denser, taller street canyons with lower sky view trap longwave radiation and suppress sensible cooling, producing a larger nocturnal temperature excess.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rural surfaces have comparable or higher thermal mass than the urban surfaces, the storage-release asymmetry vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If sky view factor in the city is high and longwave radiation escapes freely, the nocturnal cooling rate would match the countryside and the gap would not persist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speeds are high, turbulent mixing would homogenize the urban and rural boundary layers, erasing the radiative-trapping temperature excess regardless of sky view factor.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If anthropogenic heat emissions dominate, the observed cross-city variation would correlate with energy consumption rather than built density or street canyon geometry.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, concrete, asphalt, and masonry absorb solar radiation. Their high thermal mass and heat capacity mean the impervious urban fabric stores more sensible heat than moist, vegetated countryside. After sunset, rural surfaces cool rapidly via unimpeded longwave emission to the sky (high sky view factor). In contrast, dense urban street canyons have a reduced sky view factor: the upward longwave flux from the street is intercepted by building walls and re-emitted downward. This radiative trapping slows the nocturnal cooling rate of the stored urban heat. The remaining sensible heat is released into the urban boundary layer throughout the night, maintaining air several degrees warmer. Cities with denser, taller buildings (lower sky view factor) thus exhibit a stronger night-time UHI than sprawling, low-rise cities.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
